content: Nocturnal enuresis, commonly referred to as bedwetting, is a condition that can cause significant social stigma and emotional distress. It affects approximately 15% to 20% of five-year-old children and persists in up to 2% of young adults. While many cases resolve spontaneously over time, the psychological and social burden on affected children can be substantial. Various pharmacological treatments, including desmopressin, tricyclic antidepressants, and other drugs, have been explored to manage this condition. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of drugs other than desmopressin and tricyclic antidepressants in treating nocturnal enuresis in children. Additionally, the review aimed to compare these drugs with other interventions, such as behavioral therapies. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Incontinence Group Specialised Register of trials, which includes data from MEDLINE and CENTRAL, as of December 15, 2011. Both published and unpublished randomized and quasi-randomized trials were considered. Reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed to identify additional studies. The inclusion criteria for this review encompassed all randomized trials involving children up to 16 years of age who were treated with drugs (excluding desmopressin and tricyclics) for nocturnal enuresis. Eligible studies compared these drugs to placebo, other drugs, or behavioral interventions. Trials that included children with daytime urinary incontinence or organic conditions were also included if the primary focus was nocturnal enuresis. However, studies exclusively addressing daytime wetting or adult populations were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the included trials and extracted data. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion with a third reviewer. A total of 40 randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials met the inclusion criteria, involving 2,440 children, of whom 1,780 received an active drug other than desmopressin or a tricyclic. Across these trials, 31 different drugs or drug classes were tested. However, the trials were generally small in size and of poor methodological quality. There was a notable lack of data on outcomes after treatment discontinuation. When comparing drugs to placebo, certain medications demonstrated some efficacy in reducing the number of children who failed to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights. For example: Indomethacin showed a risk ratio (RR) of 0.36 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.16 to 0.79). Diazepam had an RR of 0.22 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.46). Mestorelone demonstrated an RR of 0.32 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.62). Atomoxetine showed an RR of 0.81 (95% CI 0.70 to 0.94). While indomethacin and diclofenac were more effective than placebo during treatment, they were less effective than desmopressin and were associated with a higher likelihood of adverse effects. None of the medications studied were effective in reducing relapse rates, although this outcome was only reported in five placebo-controlled trials. When comparing drugs to other drugs, combination therapy with imipramine and oxybutynin was found to be more effective than imipramine monotherapy (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.94). Additionally, combination therapy resulted in significantly lower relapse rates compared to imipramine monotherapy (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.77). However, data on outcomes after treatment withdrawal remained limited. When comparing drugs to behavioral therapy, bedwetting alarms were found to be superior to amphetamine (RR 2.2, 95% CI 1.12 to 4.29), oxybutynin (RR 3.25, 95% CI 1.77 to 5.98), and a combination of oxybutynin and holding exercises (RR 3.3, 95% CI 1.84 to 6.18) in reducing the number of children who failed to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights. Adverse effects of the drugs were reported in 19 trials, while 17 trials did not adequately report side effects. The authors concluded that there was insufficient evidence to determine whether the included drugs were effective in curing bedwetting when used alone. Limited evidence suggested that desmopressin, imipramine, and enuresis alarm therapy were more effective than the drugs included in this review. Previous reviews have demonstrated the efficacy of desmopressin, tricyclics, and alarm interventions during treatment. There was also evidence to suggest that combination therapy with anticholinergic agents could enhance the effectiveness of established treatments, such as imipramine, desmopressin, and enuresis alarms, by reducing relapse rates by approximately 20%. However, it was not possible to identify specific characteristics of children who might benefit most from combination therapy. The authors emphasized the need for future studies to rigorously evaluate the role of combination therapy compared to established treatments in adequately powered trials.
